net sales.heading: Sources of Revenues
net sales.text:
We operate on a not-for-profit basis and, accordingly, seek only to generate revenues sufficient to recover our cost of service and to generate margins sufficient to establish reasonable reserves and meet certain financial coverage requirements. Our primary source of revenue is the sale of capacity and energy to our members for a portion of their energy requirements. We may also sell capacity and energy to non-members. Capacity revenues are the revenues we receive for providing electric service whether or not our generation and purchased power resources are dispatched to produce electricity. Energy revenues are the revenues we receive by selling electricity that we generate or purchase.

We have assigned fixed percentage capacity cost responsibilities to our members for all of our generation resources. Each member has contractually agreed to pay us for the electric capacity assigned to it based on its individual fixed percentage capacity cost responsibility.

Each member is also contractually obligated to pay us for electric energy we provide to it based on individual usage.

intro.text: We are a Georgia electric membership corporation (an EMC) incorporated in 1974 and headquartered in metropolitan Atlanta. We are owned by our 38 retail electric distribution cooperative members. Our principal business is providing wholesale electric power to our members. As with cooperatives generally, we operate on a not-for-profit basis. We are one of the largest electric cooperatives in the United States in terms of revenues, assets, kilowatt-hour sales to members and, through our members, consumers served. We are also the second largest power supplier in the state of Georgia. As of December 31, 2025, we had 401 employees.

lines.name: Cash and cash equivalents
lines.why: Cash can repay debt or be paid out: a financial asset. Cash needed to run the business is operating; move it if you know how much.

lines.name: Short-term investments
lines.why: Securities held for the cash they will return: financial.

lines.name: Long-term investments
lines.why: Securities held for their return: financial. A stake in another business that is part of operations is operating.

lines.name: Receivables
lines.why: Owed by customers for sales: operating.

lines.name: Prepaid and other current assets
lines.why: Prepayments and other operating items: operating.

lines.name: Operating lease right-of-use assets
lines.why: Leased stores, offices and equipment used in the business: operating.

lines.name: Equity-method investments
lines.why: Stakes in associated businesses, usually part of operations. Financial if held as an investment.

lines.name: Accounts payable
lines.why: Owed to suppliers for operations: operating.

lines.name: Deferred revenue
lines.why: Customers' payments ahead of delivery: operating.

lines.name: Other current liabilities
lines.why: Other operating items due within a year: operating.

lines.name: Current portion of long-term debt
lines.why: Borrowed money falling due within a year: financial.

lines.name: Finance lease liabilities
lines.why: Leases that work like a loan for the asset: financial.

lines.name: Operating lease liabilities
lines.why: Rent owed on leases used in the business: operating by default. Move it to financing to treat leases like debt (if the balance sheet has no lease line of its own, they sit inside other liabilities).

lines.name: Deferred revenue, non-current
lines.why: Customers' payments for later years: operating.

lines.name: Other assets, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total assets minus the lines above: assets the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

lines.name: Other liabilities, not tagged separately
lines.why: Total liabilities minus the lines above: liabilities the company tags its own way. Operating by default.

s.t: In 2025, one of our members, Jackson EMC, accounted for approximately 18% of our total revenues.
Each of our other members accounted for less than 10% of our total revenues in 2025.
Jackson's revenues of $457.9 million to us in 2025 under its wholesale power contract accounted for approximately 18.0% of our total revenues.
Colquitt's revenues of $52.5 million to us in 2025 under its wholesale power contract accounted for approximately 2.1% of our total revenues.
Coweta-Fayette's revenues of $111.5 million to us in 2025 under its wholesale power contract accounted for approximately 4.4% of our total revenues.
Hart's revenues of $36.7 million to us in 2025 under its wholesale power contract accounted for approximately 1.4% of our total revenues.
Central Georgia's revenues of $99.4 million to us in 2025 under its wholesale power contract accounted for approximately 3.9% of our total revenues.
The timing and amount of any actual return of capital to the members depends on the financial goals of the cooperative and the cooperative's loan and security agreements.
Our members satisfy all of their power requirements above their purchase obligations to us with purchases from other suppliers.

Historically, federal loan programs administered by the Rural Utilities Service, an agency of the United States Department of Agriculture, have provided the principal source of financing for electric cooperatives.
Loans guaranteed by the Rural Utilities Service and made by the Federal Financing Bank have been a major source of funding for us.
Georgia Transmission provides transmission services to its members for delivery of its members' power purchases from us and other power suppliers.
We also purchase from Georgia System Operations services that it purchases from Georgia Power under the Control Area Compact, which we co-signed with Georgia System Operations.
Further, many of our members' third-party suppliers also rely on generation sources that emit greenhouse gases.
Our success depends on the people who are part of our company.
Our members are the principal suppliers for the power needs of rural Georgia.
We depend on the revenue we receive from our members pursuant to the wholesale power contracts to cover the costs of operation of our power supply business and satisfy our debt service obligations.
Historically, federal loan programs providing direct and guaranteed loans from the Rural Utilities Service to electric cooperatives have been a major source of funding for the members.
Georgia Transmission provides transmission services to our members for delivery of our members' power purchases from us and other power suppliers.

Georgia System Operations has contracts with each of its members, including Georgia Transmission and us, to provide to them the services that it in turn purchases from Georgia Power under the Control Area Compact, which we co-signed with Georgia System Operations.

See "OGLETHORPE POWER CORPORATION – Wholesale Power Contracts." Our members satisfy all of their requirements above their purchase obligations to us with purchases from other suppliers as described below.

However, the regulation of air emissions has been and is expected to continue to be fluid, and additional emissions reduction requirements could be imposed on major sources within Georgia, including at our power plants, to remedy any local and interstate transport air quality problems.

The cost impact of future legislation, regulation, judicial interpretations of existing laws or regulations, or international obligations will depend upon the specific requirements thereof and cannot be determined at this time.
We rely on the successful operation of our generation facilities to provide our members’ energy needs.
We rely on these third parties for the continued operation of these facilities to avoid potential interruptions in service from these facilities.

In recent years, some banking and insurance companies have also voluntarily implemented policies to limit lending to, investing in and insuring utilities that significantly rely on coal-fired generation assets.

The ultimate impact of an early retirement on us and our members would depend on several factors, including the proposed retirement date, our ability to recover costs after the retirement date, the price and availability of any replacement energy and cannot be determined at this time.
As we have financed generation assets in the past, we rely on external funding to finance additional generation resources.
Further, our generation assets rely on an integrated transmission system to deliver power to our members, and a disruption of this transmission system could negatively impact our ability to do so.

Even in an active trading market, future prices of our debt securities will depend on several factors, including prevailing interest rates, the then-current ratings assigned to the debt securities, the number of holders of the debt securities, the amount of our debt securities outstanding, the market for similar securities and our financial and operating results.
Georgia Power is the largest supplier of electric energy in the State of Georgia.
Our primary source of liquidity is a $1.275 billion unsecured credit facility that extends through May 2029 and supports our commercial paper program.
Our primary source of revenue is the sale of capacity and energy to our members for a portion of their energy requirements.

The primary sources of our long-term debt consist of first mortgage bonds, pollution control revenue bonds and long-term debt issued by the Federal Financing Bank that is guaranteed by the Rural Utilities Service or the U.S. Department of Energy.
